hero.title: The SOLID Principles
task.1.title: S - Single Responsibility: the feeding card
task.1.context:
You are writing the little program the animal shelter uses at feeding time. A volunteer walks the aisle with a tablet, and for each cat it shows a card: `FEED` if the cat is due a meal, `FULL` if it is not.

The rule the vet gave you is simple - **six or more hours since the last meal means the cat needs feeding.**

Write the obvious thing. One class, one method: hand it the hours, get the card back. There is nothing clever here and nothing wrong with it. Get it working, then we will change it.
task.1.goal.0: **Write the method.** Give `Cat` a `string CheckAndSign(int hoursSinceMeal)`.
task.1.goal.1: **Use the rule.** Six or more hours means `"FEED"`. Anything less means `"FULL"`.
task.1.goal.2: **Print one card.** `Main` already asks about a cat that last ate seven hours ago, so the output is `FEED`.
task.2.title: S - Single Responsibility: the vet changes the rule
task.2.context:
Your program went into the shelter and worked. Two things happened since.

The front desk asked for a **number** - how many cats are waiting to be fed - to put on the whiteboard. `CheckAndSign` only hands out the words `"FEED"` and `"FULL"`, and you cannot add up words, so somebody wrote the rule out a second time inside `FrontDesk.HungryCount`. It works. Nobody thought about it twice.

Now the vet has changed her mind: **four hours, not six.**

Make that change. That is the whole task. Then look at what it cost.
task.2.goal.0: **Make the vet's change.** A cat is hungry after four hours now, not six.
task.2.goal.1: **Everything has to agree.** The cards and the tally answer the same question, so both have to move. Miss one and nothing crashes - the program just lies.
task.2.goal.2: **Run it.** Three cats at seven, five and two hours print `FEED`, `FEED`, `FULL`, then `2 need feeding`.
task.3.title: S - Single Responsibility: one rule, one place
task.3.context:
Count what that change touched: two edits, in two classes, for one decision by the vet. And if you had changed only one of them, nothing would have gone red. The program would have printed two `FEED` cards next to a tally reading `1`, and nobody would have known until a cat went hungry.

That is what the **S** in SOLID is about, and it is not tidiness. `Cat` had two jobs - deciding whether the cat is hungry, and writing the card - and because the deciding was sealed inside a method that returned words, the front desk could not reuse it and copied it instead. Two jobs in one method is how one rule ends up in two places.

So give each job a home of its own:
- `Cat` remembers its own hours and answers one question - am I hungry?
- `FeedingSign` knows the two words, and turns a yes-or-no into one of them.
- `FrontDesk` counts, by **asking each cat** rather than by knowing the rule.

Now make the vet's change again - four hours - in this shape. The output is the same as the last card. Count the edits this time.
task.3.goal.0: **Let the cat hold its own state.** `Cat` takes its hours in a constructor and answers `bool IsHungry()`.
task.3.goal.1: **Give the wording a home.** `FeedingSign` turns that yes-or-no into `"FEED"` or `"FULL"`.
task.3.goal.2: **Let the desk ask, not know.** `FrontDesk` counts by asking each cat, so the rule is not written here.
task.3.goal.4: **Same change, same output.** Four hours, and it still prints `FEED`, `FEED`, `FULL`, `2 need feeding` - but the rule is written once.
task.4.title: O - Open/Closed: add an animal without editing
task.4.context:
This is the **O** in SOLID: Open/Closed. Code should be open to new behaviour but closed to edits - you add a case without reopening what already works.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? You just felt the answer. Every time you edit a working method to bolt on a case, you put the cases that already passed at risk, and you have to retest all of them. Here `AnimalVoice.Speak` grows another `if` for every animal. Add a cow and you reopen the very method the cats and dogs depend on.

The fix: give each animal its own class behind a shared `IAnimal`. A new animal becomes a new file, and the old ones are never touched - so they cannot break.
task.4.goal.0: **Name the promise.** Declare `interface IAnimal` with `string Speak()`.
task.4.goal.1: **One class per animal.** Write a `Cat : IAnimal` that speaks `"Meow"`.
task.4.goal.3: **Retire the if-chain.** `AnimalVoice` and its `kind ==` checks are gone.
task.4.goal.4: **Run it.** `Main` holds a `Cat` in an `IAnimal` variable, and the output stays `Meow`.
task.5.title: L - Liskov Substitution: the penguin that can't fly
task.5.context:
This is the **L** in SOLID: Liskov Substitution. Any subtype has to be usable anywhere its parent is, with no surprises.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? Inheritance looks like free reuse, but a child that cannot keep the parent's promise is a landmine. A `Penguin` under `Bird` still has a `Fly()`, so it throws - and the code that breaks is not the penguin's. It is the keeper's loop, which was written before penguins arrived, has not been touched since, and now crashes because of a class it has never heard of. Run the starter and watch it happen.

The fix: drop the false is-a. Let both share a small `IMover` and return the move each animal can actually make.
task.5.goal.0: **Promise only what everyone can keep.** Declare `interface IMover` with `string Move()`.
task.5.goal.1: **A sparrow flies.** Write a `Sparrow : IMover` whose `Move()` returns `"Fly"`.
task.5.goal.2: **A penguin swims.** Write a `Penguin : IMover` whose `Move()` returns `"Swim"` - a real answer, not a `throw`.
task.5.goal.3: **Nothing can betray a caller.** The `Bird` base is gone, and so is every `throw`.
task.5.goal.4: **Run it.** `Main` moves a `Penguin` through an `IMover`, and the output is `Swim`.
task.6.title: I - Interface Segregation: a fish that only swims
task.6.context:
This is the **I** in SOLID: Interface Segregation. No class should be forced to carry methods it never uses.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? Because a fat interface makes everyone who implements it your problem. `IAnimalActions` demands `Walk`, `Swim` and `Fly`, so `Fish` has two methods that exist only to throw. Now add `Climb()` to that interface: every animal in the shelter stops compiling, including the ones that will never climb anything. One line, and the whole codebase is your afternoon.

The fix: one interface per job, and each animal implements only what it actually does.
task.6.goal.0: **Split the fat interface.** Declare `IWalker` with `string Walk()`.
task.6.goal.3: **Only what it does.** `Fish : ISwimmer` - with no `Walk` and no `Fly` on it at all.
task.6.goal.4: **Retire the fat one.** `IAnimalActions` is gone, and so are the throwing stubs.
task.6.goal.5: **Run it.** `Main` swims a `Fish` through an `ISwimmer`, and the output stays `swim`.
task.7.title: D - Dependency Inversion: a keeper you can test
task.7.context:
This is the **D** in SOLID: Dependency Inversion. Depend on what you need, and take it from outside instead of building it yourself.

Why bother - isn't this overengineering? Try writing a test for this `Keeper`. It builds its own `ConsoleLog`, so the only way to find out whether feeding was recorded is to run it and read the console with your eyes. Swap the console for a real database or a real email and it gets worse: your test now needs the database. A class that builds its own collaborators cannot be checked without them.

The fix: let `Keeper` ask for an `ILog` and be handed one. Real code hands it a `ConsoleLog`; a test hands it a fake that just remembers what it was told.
task.7.goal.0: **Name what the keeper needs.** Declare `interface ILog` with `void Write(string message)`.
task.7.goal.1: **Keep the real one.** `ConsoleLog : ILog` still prints to the console.
task.7.goal.2: **Hand it in, don't build it.** `Keeper` takes an `ILog` in its constructor and stores it.
task.7.goal.3: **Nothing inside `Keeper` says `new ConsoleLog()`.** That is the line that welded it to the console.
task.7.goal.4: **Run it.** `Main` builds the keeper with a `ConsoleLog`, and the output stays `cat fed`.
task.8.title: What you learned
task.8.context: The five habits in one place - what each one fixes.
task.8.summaryIntro: None of these are rules for their own sake. Each one saves you a headache the day the code has to change - which is why you met the headache first:
task.8.summaryItems.0.title: S - Single Responsibility -
task.8.summaryItems.0.text: One class, one job. You changed the feeding rule twice: once in a shape where it lived in two places, and once in a shape where it lived in one. The two-place version could go wrong without going red. That is the whole argument.
task.8.summaryItems.1.title: O - Open/Closed -
task.8.summaryItems.1.text: Add a new animal without touching the old code. Instead of another branch in an `if`-chain, you write a new class behind `IAnimal`. The code that already worked is never reopened, so it cannot break.
task.8.summaryItems.2.title: L - Liskov Substitution -
task.8.summaryItems.2.text: A subtype has to work anywhere its parent does. A `Penguin` under `Bird` broke that - it threw on `Fly()`, and the code that crashed belonged to somebody who had never heard of penguins. Drop the false claim and let both share a promise they can keep.
task.8.summaryItems.3.title: I - Interface Segregation -
task.8.summaryItems.3.text: Don't make a class carry methods it never uses. Split the fat interface into `IWalker`, `ISwimmer` and `IFlyer`, and adding a `Climb()` stops being everyone's problem.
task.8.summaryItems.4.title: D - Dependency Inversion -
task.8.summaryItems.4.text: Ask for an interface and take it from outside instead of building the real thing yourself. Once the `ILog` is handed in, a test can hand in a fake.
task.8.summaryClose: So when someone calls this overengineering, they are half right, and it is worth being honest about which half. The cost of an abstraction is paid today; the benefit only arrives if the change arrives. Scatter interfaces everywhere up front and you have paid for nothing. The useful rule is narrower: **abstract along the line that has already changed once.** The feeding rule changed - so it earned a home of its own.
concept.pr-open-closed.def: Code that is open to new behaviour by adding a type, and closed to editing what already works.
concept.pr-liskov-substitution.def: A subtype must be usable anywhere its base is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions.
concept.pr-interface-segregation.def: Keeping interfaces small and focused, so a type is not forced to implement methods it does not need.
concept.pr-dependency-inversion.def: High-level code depending on an abstraction rather than a concrete detail, so the detail can change freely.
